newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain April CPI seen breaking 2 percent barrier.
newsitem.headline: Spain April CPI seen breaking 2 percent barrier.

text.p: The falling trend in Spanish inflation is not yet over and both April and May data will likely set fresh records, analysts said on Wednesday.
Financial analysts are revising down their forecasts ahead of the release on May 14 of the April data, expected to break the two percent threshold.
Banco Bilbao Viczaya (BBV) said on Wednesday that the April yearly inflation rate should fall to 1.9 percent, with a record low expected in May at 1.5 percent.
A Morgan Stanley report on Tuesday said inflation was expected at 1.8 percent in April and 1.7 percent in May.
A week before that, Bank of America in Madrid said it was forecasting May data to be at 1.7 percent.
Spain's consumer price index has fallen from 3.2 percent in December 1996, hitting a near-30 year low in March at 2.2 percent.
Despite the general view that this record will be broken first in April, than again in May, analysts have started to consider the official 1997 target of 2.6 percent too high.

"Spain's inflation will break two percent in April, it will be around 1.5 percent in May and will end the year around two percent, well below the government's target of 2.6 percent," BBV said in a note to clients.
Technical reasons, such as a favourable comparison with the year-ago period, are supporting the view of a declining CPI in April and May.

"After tame March data, it is not only clear Spain will reach the Maastricht criteria -- not being more than 1.5 points higher than the average of the three countries with lowest inflation -- but also that the inflation rate could stay around two percent during the whole year," a study of the independent group of the economists ERISTE said.
One year ago increases in white-meat prices after the "mad-cow" outbreak should offer favourable comparisons in the food sector, a note from Caja de Catalunia said.
Prices of fresh food are expected to continue on a very tame trend while processed food should be kept lower by olive oil prices, which has a strong weight in the index basket.
But, while some analysts suggest that further falls in the Spain's CPI will be followed by further official rate cuts, not all agree.
"(This) is not necessarily true because the most drastic fall in the price index will be in the more volatile components, such as energy and food," an Argentaria note said.
Currently Spain's official rate stands at 5.50 percent, after the central bank already sanctioned three 25-basis point cuts this year so far.
The Bank of Spain started its current cycle of rate reductions on December 22 1995, when it cut its official rate to nine percent from 9.25 percent.
